new_questions.question_text: Which of the following motivations are MOST commonly associated with hacktivist threat actors? (Select THREE.)
choices: Service disruption to draw public attention
Revenge against an organization perceived as unethical
Long-term espionage on behalf of a foreign government
Acquiring intellectual property for competitive advantage
correct_choice_texts: Service disruption to draw public attention
Revenge against an organization perceived as unethical
new_questions.hint: Hacktivists are ideologically driven, not profit-driven.
new_questions.explanation: Per SY0-701 Objective 2.1, hacktivist motivations center on philosophical/political beliefs, disruption/chaos, and revenge. Long-term espionage and IP theft characterize nation-state actors; financial extortion characterizes organized crime. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.1 (Motivations) and MITRE ATT&CK Groups (e.g., Anonymous-associated activity).
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.1 (Motivations bullet group)

new_questions.question_text: Which of the following attributes distinguish a nation-state advanced persistent threat (APT) from less-resourced actors? (Select THREE.)
choices: Long dwell time and persistent access objectives
Reliance on publicly available script kits
Motivation limited to immediate financial gain
correct_choice_texts: Long dwell time and persistent access objectives
new_questions.hint: APT = Advanced (custom tools), Persistent (long-term), Threat (well-resourced).
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.1 lists nation-state actors with high capability and resources; MITRE characterizes APT groups by long dwell time, custom malware, and strategic targeting. Public scripts and opportunistic targeting describe unskilled attackers. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.1 and MITRE ATT&CK Groups (APT28, APT29, etc.).

new_questions.question_text: Which of the following are classified as human (social engineering) threat vectors in SY0-701 Objective 2.2? (Select THREE.)
new_questions.hint: Human vectors target the person, not a port, hypervisor, or default config.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.2 enumerates human vectors/social engineering: phishing, vishing, smishing, misinformation/disinformation, impersonation, business email compromise, pretexting, watering hole, brand impersonation, and typosquatting, plus MFA fatigue. Open ports, VM escape, and default credentials are non-human vectors. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.2 (Human vectors/social engineering).

new_questions.question_text: Which of the following are examples of message-based threat vectors? (Select THREE.)
new_questions.hint: Message-based = arrives as a message in an inbox/channel.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.2 explicitly lists message-based vectors: email, short message service (SMS), and instant messaging (IM). USB is a removable-device vector; Bluetooth pairing is an unsecure-network vector; open ports are an attack-surface vector. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.2 (Message-based).
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.2 (Message-based vectors)

new_questions.question_text: Which of the following are application-layer vulnerability types listed in SY0-701 Objective 2.3? (Select THREE.)
new_questions.hint: Application vulnerabilities live in the program's own code or runtime.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.3 'Application' bullet enumerates memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions (including time-of-check/time-of-use), and malicious update. VM escape is virtualization (CWE-1041); EOL firmware is hardware/legacy; jailbreaking is mobile. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.3 (Application), MITRE CWE-120 (buffer overflow), CWE-367 (TOCTOU).

new_questions.question_text: Which of the following are virtualization-specific vulnerabilities relevant to SY0-701 Objective 2.3? (Select TWO.)
choices: SQL injection in the guest application
Buffer overflow in a desktop application
new_questions.hint: Think hypervisor boundary failures and memory not zeroed between VMs.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.3 'Virtualization' lists virtual machine escape and resource reuse as the canonical hypervisor-layer vulnerabilities. SQL injection is web-application, sideloading is mobile, and buffer overflow is application. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.3 (Virtualization) and NIST SP 800-125 (hypervisor security).
sources: NIST SP 800-125 – Security for Full Virtualization Technologies

new_questions.question_text: Which of the following are listed as indicators of malicious activity in SY0-701 Objective 2.4? (Select THREE.)
new_questions.hint: Look for anomalies and gaps, not normal benign telemetry.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.4 'Indicators' lists account lockout, concurrent session usage, blocked content, impossible travel, resource consumption, resource inaccessibility, out-of-cycle logging, published/documented, and missing logs. Patched OS and routine backups are benign. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.4 (Indicators) and NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.2.
sources: NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.2 (Detection and analysis – signs of incident)

new_questions.question_text: Which of the following are password / credential attacks listed under SY0-701 Objective 2.4? (Select THREE.)
new_questions.hint: These are all credential/cryptographic attacks, not memory or web injection.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.4 lists password attacks (spraying, brute force) under credential replay/abuse and cryptographic attacks including birthday and collision. Buffer overflow and XSS are application vulnerabilities (§2.3); jailbreaking is a mobile vulnerability. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.4 (Password attacks / Cryptographic attacks) and NIST SP 800-63B §5.1.1.

new_questions.question_text: Which of the following are mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise under SY0-701 Objective 2.5? (Select THREE.)
new_questions.hint: Mitigations reduce risk; the other options are attacks or vulnerabilities.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.5 enumerates segmentation, access control (ACL/permissions), application allow list, isolation, patching, encryption, monitoring, least privilege, configuration enforcement, and decommissioning. Phishing is a §2.2 vector; VM escape and race condition are §2.3 vulnerabilities. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 and NIST SP 800-53r5 controls AC-6 (Least Privilege), SI-2 (Flaw Remediation), SC-7 (Boundary Protection).

new_questions.question_text: Which of the following are valid hardening targets explicitly listed in SY0-701 Objective 2.5? (Select THREE.)
new_questions.hint: Hardening targets are systems and devices you can configure.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.5 'Hardening targets' explicitly lists mobile devices, workstations, switches, routers, cloud infrastructure, servers, ICS/SCADA, embedded systems, RTOS, and IoT devices. Threat feeds and reports are inputs/artifacts, not hardening targets. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 (Hardening targets) and CIS Benchmarks / DISA STIGs.
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 (Hardening targets)

new_questions.question_text: True or False: SY0-701 Objective 2.1 lists 'shadow IT' as a category of threat actor.
new_questions.hint: Re-read the bullet list of actor types in 2.1.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.1 explicitly enumerates threat actors: nation-state, unskilled attacker, hacktivist, insider threat, organized crime, and shadow IT. Shadow IT — unsanctioned systems/services introduced by employees outside IT governance — is treated as a threat actor on the exam. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.1 (Threat actors).
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.1 (Threat actors)

new_questions.question_text: True or False: An 'unskilled attacker' in SY0-701 Objective 2.1 typically relies on pre-built tools or scripts rather than developing custom exploits.
new_questions.hint: Think 'script kiddie.'
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.1 characterizes the unskilled attacker (script kiddie) by low capability/resources, using publicly available tooling rather than custom development. Sophistication and custom tooling characterize nation-state APTs. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.1 (Attributes of actors).
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.1 (Attributes of actors)

new_questions.question_text: True or False: 'MFA fatigue' — repeatedly pushing authentication prompts until a user approves one — is classified by SY0-701 Objective 2.2 as a human (social engineering) threat vector.
new_questions.hint: The attack relies on annoying a human into clicking approve.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.2 lists MFA fatigue (a.k.a. push-bombing) under human/social-engineering vectors because success requires user interaction (approving a push). MITRE ATT&CK tracks this as T1621 Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.2 and MITRE ATT&CK T1621.

new_questions.question_text: True or False: Default credentials shipped on a device are NOT considered an attack surface under SY0-701 Objective 2.2.
new_questions.hint: If the credentials are publicly documented, anyone on the network can try them.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.2 explicitly lists 'default credentials' as an attack surface. Vendor-default usernames and passwords are widely published and routinely abused (e.g., Mirai's success against IoT). The correct answer is False — default credentials ARE an attack surface. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.2 (Attack surfaces) and NIST SP 800-53r5 IA-5.
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.2 (Attack surfaces)

new_questions.question_text: True or False: A zero-day vulnerability, by definition, has no vendor-provided patch available at the time it is exploited or disclosed.
new_questions.hint: The vendor has had zero days to prepare a fix.
new_questions.explanation: Per SY0-701 §2.3, a zero-day is a vulnerability unknown to the vendor (or for which no patch yet exists), giving defenders zero days of warning. NIST defines a zero-day similarly in SP 800-150 (Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing). See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.3 (Zero-day) and NIST SP 800-150.
sources: NIST SP 800-150 – Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

new_questions.question_text: True or False: A time-of-check/time-of-use (TOCTOU) flaw is classified by SY0-701 Objective 2.3 as a memory-injection vulnerability.
new_questions.hint: TOCTOU is about timing windows between two operations.
new_questions.explanation: TOCTOU is a race-condition vulnerability — the state of a resource changes between the check and the use — not a memory-injection vulnerability. SY0-701 §2.3 lists race conditions (including TOCTOU) as a distinct sub-bullet from memory injection. MITRE CWE-367 catalogs TOCTOU explicitly. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.3 (Application – Race conditions) and MITRE CWE-367.

new_questions.question_text: True or False: A logic bomb is malware that executes its payload only when a specific trigger condition (such as a date, account state, or event) is met.
new_questions.hint: The 'bomb' detonates on a condition, not immediately.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.4 lists logic bombs as conditionally-activated malware. They lie dormant until a logical trigger (date, missing employee record, file deletion) fires the payload. MITRE ATT&CK tracks logic-bomb-style behavior under T1059 / T1546.005 conditional execution. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.4 (Malware – Logic bomb).
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.4 (Malware attacks)
MITRE ATT&CK T1546 – Event Triggered Execution

new_questions.question_text: True or False: 'Impossible travel' — successful logins from two geographically distant locations within a span of time that no human could traverse — is listed as an indicator of malicious activity in SY0-701 Objective 2.4.
new_questions.hint: It is one of the named indicators in 2.4.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.4 explicitly lists 'impossible travel' under Indicators of malicious activity. It is a high-fidelity signal of credential compromise commonly surfaced by SIEMs and UEBA platforms. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.4 (Indicators) and NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.2.

new_questions.question_text: True or False: Application allow-listing (whitelisting) operates on a default-deny model — only explicitly approved executables are permitted to run.
new_questions.hint: If a binary is not on the list, it does not run.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.5 lists application allow list as a mitigation. By design, allow-listing denies execution by default and permits only known-good binaries (by hash, path, or publisher). NIST SP 800-167 (Guide to Application Whitelisting) formalizes this default-deny posture. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 and NIST SP 800-167 §2.
sources: NIST SP 800-167 – Guide to Application Whitelisting

new_questions.question_text: True or False: Decommissioning a legacy or end-of-life system is NOT considered a mitigation technique under SY0-701 Objective 2.5.
new_questions.hint: Removing an unpatchable system removes its risk.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.5 explicitly lists decommissioning as a mitigation technique. Retiring an EOL/unpatchable system eliminates the residual risk that monitoring or compensating controls cannot fully neutralize. The statement is therefore False. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 and NIST SP 800-88r1 (Media sanitization on decommissioning).
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 (Mitigation techniques)
NIST SP 800-88r1 – Guidelines for Media Sanitization

new_questions.question_text: Place the seven phases of the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain in the correct order, from earliest to latest.
ordered_choice_texts: Reconnaissance
Weaponization
Delivery
Exploitation
Installation
Command and Control
Actions on Objectives
new_questions.hint: An attacker must first study the target, then build, then deliver, before code can run.
new_questions.explanation: The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain defines seven sequential phases: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control (C2), and Actions on Objectives. It is referenced in SY0-701 §2.4 as a model for understanding attack progression. See Lockheed Martin – 'The Cyber Kill Chain' (https://www.lockheedmartin.com/en-us/capabilities/cyber/cyber-kill-chain.html).

new_questions.question_text: Place the following MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise tactics in the typical macro-order an adversary progresses through them, from earliest to latest.
ordered_choice_texts: Reconnaissance
Initial Access
Execution
Privilege Escalation
Lateral Movement
Exfiltration
new_questions.hint: Recon happens before access; movement and exfiltration come after a foothold and elevation.
new_questions.explanation: The MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise matrix orders tactics left-to-right roughly chronologically: Reconnaissance → Resource Development → Initial Access → Execution → Persistence → Privilege Escalation → Defense Evasion → Credential Access → Discovery → Lateral Movement → Collection → Command and Control → Exfiltration → Impact. The six selected here follow that macro-order. See MITRE ATT&CK Matrix for Enterprise (https://attack.mitre.org/matrices/enterprise/) — referenced as a threat-modeling framework under SY0-701 §2.4.

new_questions.question_text: A new critical CVE is announced for a server in production. Place the following vulnerability-mitigation lifecycle steps in the correct order.
choices: Detection of the affected asset via vulnerability scan
Containment by network segmentation or temporary isolation
Decommissioning if the component is end-of-life and cannot be patched
ordered_choice_texts: Detection of the affected asset via vulnerability scan
Containment by network segmentation or temporary isolation
Patch deployment from the vendor
Verification scan and continuous monitoring
Decommissioning if the component is end-of-life and cannot be patched
new_questions.hint: You cannot mitigate what you have not detected; verify before retiring.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.5 lists segmentation, isolation, patching, monitoring, and decommissioning as mitigation techniques and §4.3 describes vulnerability management lifecycle: identification → analysis → response → reporting. The order is detect → contain → patch → verify → decommission (only if unpatchable). See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 / §4.3 and NIST SP 800-40r4 (Guide to Enterprise Patch Management).
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 and §4.3
NIST SP 800-40r4 – Guide to Enterprise Patch Management

new_questions.question_text: Place the stages of a software supply-chain compromise (SolarWinds-style) in the correct order.
choices: Adversary compromises the software vendor's build environment
Malicious code is inserted into a legitimate signed update
Customers download and install the trojanized update
Backdoor activates and beacons to attacker command and control
Adversary pivots laterally and exfiltrates customer data
ordered_choice_texts: Adversary compromises the software vendor's build environment
Malicious code is inserted into a legitimate signed update
Customers download and install the trojanized update
Backdoor activates and beacons to attacker command and control
Adversary pivots laterally and exfiltrates customer data
new_questions.hint: The vendor is breached first; downstream customers are the second-order victims.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.2 'Supply chain' and §2.3 'Malicious update' describe this exact chain: adversary compromises a trusted vendor, plants malicious code in a signed update, customers ingest it, the backdoor activates, then the adversary moves laterally and exfiltrates. CISA's SUNBURST advisory documents this sequence for SolarWinds. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.2/§2.3, CISA Alert AA20-352A, and MITRE ATT&CK T1195.002 (Compromise Software Supply Chain).
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.2 (Supply chain) and §2.3
CISA Alert AA20-352A – Advanced Persistent Threat Compromise of Government Agencies, Critical Infrastructure, and Private Sector Organizations
MITRE ATT&CK T1195.002 – Compromise Software Supply Chain

new_questions.question_text: Place the following server hardening steps in the order they should generally be performed when standing up a new system.
choices: Inventory the asset and its role
Apply CIS Benchmarks or DISA STIGs
Enroll the asset in continuous monitoring
ordered_choice_texts: Inventory the asset and its role
Establish a secure configuration baseline
Apply CIS Benchmarks or DISA STIGs
Disable unused ports and services
Remove or change default credentials
Enroll the asset in continuous monitoring
new_questions.hint: You can't harden what you haven't inventoried; monitor last so the baseline is the reference.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.5 'Hardening targets' and §4.1 secure baselines describe this flow: inventory → baseline → apply benchmark (CIS/STIG) → disable unused ports/services → eliminate defaults → continuous monitoring. NIST SP 800-128 (Security-Focused Configuration Management) formalizes the order. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 / §4.1, NIST SP 800-128, and CIS Critical Security Controls v8 (Controls 1, 4).
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 and §4.1

new_questions.question_text: According to the Carnegie Mellon CERT Insider Threat Center model, place the stages an insider typically progresses through before committing a malicious act.
choices: Action — execution of the malicious act
ordered_choice_texts: Grievance against the organization
Ideation of a harmful action
Planning the act
Preparation (acquiring access or tools)
Action — execution of the malicious act
new_questions.hint: Anger comes before idea; idea before plan; plan before preparation; preparation before action.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.1 covers insider threat actors. CERT's Insider Threat research models radicalization-style progression: grievance → ideation → planning → preparation → action. Early detection at grievance/ideation enables prevention before tools or access are acquired. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.1 and Carnegie Mellon SEI CERT Insider Threat Center (https://insights.sei.cmu.edu/insider-threat/).
sources: Carnegie Mellon SEI CERT Insider Threat Center – Common Sense Guide to Mitigating Insider Threats

new_questions.question_text: Place the typical phishing-as-a-vector chain in order, from earliest to latest.
choices: Attacker crafts a convincing lure and spoofed sender
Email is delivered to the target's inbox
User clicks the link or opens the attachment
Credentials are harvested or malware is staged on the host
Attacker establishes command and control or exfiltrates data
ordered_choice_texts: Attacker crafts a convincing lure and spoofed sender
Email is delivered to the target's inbox
User clicks the link or opens the attachment
Credentials are harvested or malware is staged on the host
Attacker establishes command and control or exfiltrates data
new_questions.hint: The lure has to exist before it can land; the user has to click before code runs.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.2 lists phishing as a message-based human vector. The chain maps onto Lockheed's kill chain: Weaponization (lure) → Delivery (email) → Exploitation (click) → Installation/Credential Access → Command and Control / Exfiltration. MITRE ATT&CK T1566 (Phishing) and T1078 (Valid Accounts) cover the post-click stages. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.2 and MITRE ATT&CK T1566.

new_questions.question_text: Place the typical stages of a ransomware attack on an enterprise workstation in the correct order.
choices: Initial access via phishing or exposed remote service
Discovery and lateral movement to high-value hosts
Encryption of files and display of the ransom note
ordered_choice_texts: Initial access via phishing or exposed remote service
Execution of the ransomware loader
Privilege escalation and credential access
Discovery and lateral movement to high-value hosts
Encryption of files and display of the ransom note
Extortion / data leak threat
new_questions.hint: The ransom note is shown only after files have been encrypted.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.4 lists ransomware under malware attacks. Modern double-extortion ransomware follows: initial access (T1566/T1133) → execution (T1059) → privilege escalation (T1068) → lateral movement (T1021) → impact via encryption (T1486) → exfiltration-driven extortion (T1567). See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.4, MITRE ATT&CK T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact), and CISA #StopRansomware Guide.
sources: MITRE ATT&CK T1486 – Data Encrypted for Impact

new_questions.question_text: Place the following steps of responsible vulnerability disclosure and patch deployment in the correct order.
choices: Researcher privately notifies the vendor (coordinated disclosure)
Vendor develops and tests a patch
Vendor publishes the patch and a CVE advisory
Customers apply the patch and verify remediation
ordered_choice_texts: Researcher discovers the vulnerability
Researcher privately notifies the vendor (coordinated disclosure)
Vendor develops and tests a patch
Vendor publishes the patch and a CVE advisory
Customers apply the patch and verify remediation
new_questions.hint: Private notification precedes public CVE; customers patch after the CVE drops.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.3 covers vulnerability classification including 'published/documented' indicators, and §4.3 covers vulnerability management. ISO/IEC 29147 (Vulnerability disclosure) and NIST SP 800-216 codify this sequence: discovery → private vendor notification → patch development → coordinated public disclosure (CVE) → customer remediation. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.3/§4.3, ISO/IEC 29147:2018, and NIST SP 800-216.
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.3 and §4.3
NIST SP 800-216 – Recommendations for Federal Vulnerability Disclosure Guidelines

new_questions.question_text: A zero-day affecting an internet-facing application is announced with no patch available yet. Place the following incident-response mitigation steps in the correct order.
choices: Detect exposure across the asset inventory
Isolate or segment the affected hosts from production
Apply a vendor-provided workaround or virtual patch (e.g., WAF rule)
Deploy the vendor patch when released and reboot the service
Run a verification scan and resume monitoring
ordered_choice_texts: Detect exposure across the asset inventory
Isolate or segment the affected hosts from production
Apply a vendor-provided workaround or virtual patch (e.g., WAF rule)
Deploy the vendor patch when released and reboot the service
Run a verification scan and resume monitoring
new_questions.hint: Without a patch, you contain first; the real patch goes in once the vendor ships it.
new_questions.explanation: SY0-701 §2.5 mitigation techniques (segmentation, isolation, patching, monitoring) combined with §4.8 incident response (containment → eradication → recovery) yield this order: detect → isolate/segment → workaround/virtual patch → vendor patch → verify and monitor. NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.3 sets containment before eradication, and SP 800-40r4 covers the patch-deployment portion. See CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 / §4.8, NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.3, NIST SP 800-40r4.
sources: CompTIA SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF §2.5 and §4.8
NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.3 – Containment, Eradication, and Recovery
NIST SP 800-40r4 – Guide to Enterprise Patch Management
